items.followUp: How does an electron change its energy when it moves between two Bohr orbits?

rubric.why: Identifies the transition in which an electron loses energy.
rubric.description: States that an electron emits energy when it moves from a higher-energy orbit to a lower-energy orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the transition and emission of energy.

rubric.why: Identifies the transition in which an electron gains energy.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy when it moves from a lower-energy orbit to a higher-energy orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the transition and absorption of energy.

modelAnswer: An electron emits energy when it jumps from a higher-energy orbit to a lower-energy orbit.
It absorbs energy when it jumps from a lower-energy orbit to a higher-energy orbit.

items.followUp: Define ionization energy and give one example of an atom forming a positive ion.

rubric.why: The definition describes the electron gain and the energy change involved.
rubric.description: Defines electron affinity as the energy released when a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a gaseous atom gains an electron to form a negative ion and energy is released.

rubric.why: A specific valid example illustrates electron affinity.
rubric.description: Gives chlorine accepting an electron to form a chloride ion as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example identifying the atom, electron gain and negative ion formed.

modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
For example: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) + energy; a chlorine atom gains an electron to form a chloride ion.

items.followUp: What is diffusion in gases? Give an example involving two gases.

rubric.why: The definition describes the spreading and mixing of gas particles.
rubric.description: Defines diffusion of gases as the spontaneous spreading and mixing of gas particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing gas particles spreading and mixing.

rubric.why: A valid example shows gases diffusing and forming a product.
rubric.description: Gives ammonia and hydrogen chloride diffusing towards each other to form ammonium chloride.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the two gases and the ammonium chloride formed.

modelAnswer: Diffusion of gases is the spontaneous spreading and mixing of gas particles.
For example, ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas diffuse towards each other and form a white ring of ammonium chloride.

items.followUp: Why does the reactivity of alkali metals increase down Group 1?

rubric.why: Increasing atomic size places the outermost electron farther from the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that atomic radius increases down the group, placing the outermost electron farther from the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased atomic size with the outer electron being farther from the nucleus.

rubric.why: The outer electron is easier to lose, which explains the increase in metallic reactivity.
rubric.description: Explains that weaker attraction makes the outer electron easier to lose, so the metal becomes more reactive.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking easier loss of the outer electron to increased reactivity.

modelAnswer: Down a group, atomic radius increases and the outermost electron is farther from the nucleus.
The attraction between the nucleus and this electron decreases, so the electron is lost more easily and the metal becomes more reactive.
